title: DbContext and Migrations
description: Learn to configure DbContext properly, use the migration system to evolve your database schema over time, and understand how EF Core tracks changes between your model and the database.

blocks.text: DbContext is the workhorse of EF Core, but how you configure and manage its lifetime matters. In ASP.NET Core applications, DbContext should be registered as a scoped service, meaning one instance per HTTP request. This allows EF Core to track changes throughout the request and ensures thread safety.

DbContextOptions carries all configuration for the context, including the database provider, connection string, and provider-specific options. You can configure these options in OnConfiguring within the DbContext class, or in Program.cs using AddDbContext.

blocks.title: Registering DbContext in Program.cs
blocks.content: Registering AppDbContext as a scoped service with a SQL Server connection string from configuration.

blocks.text: AddDbContext registers the context as scoped and ensures that any service consuming AppDbContext receives the same instance within a single request. This is critical for change tracking — entities loaded in one part of the request are tracked and can be updated or deleted later in the same request.

blocks.title: Warning: Do not inject DbContext into singletons
blocks.text: Because DbContext is scoped, injecting it into a singleton service causes runtime exceptions. If you need database access from a singleton, inject IServiceProvider and create a scope manually, or use a factory pattern.

You can configure the database connection inside the DbContext class by overriding OnConfiguring. This approach is common in console applications where Program.cs does not have the same dependency injection setup. However, for ASP.NET Core, AddDbContext is the preferred approach.

blocks.title: OnConfiguring override for a console app
blocks.content: Configuring the database connection directly inside the DbContext class.

blocks.text: OnModelCreating uses the Fluent API to configure entity properties. Here, we set a maximum length on Name, require it to be non-null, and define Price with a precision of 10 digits and 2 decimal places — common for currency columns.

As your application evolves, your database schema needs to change too. You might add a new column, rename a table, or create relationships between entities. Migrations are EF Core's system for managing these schema changes over time in a predictable, version-controlled way.

A migration is a snapshot of your model at a point in time, along with the SQL operations needed to transform the database from the previous state to the new state. Migrations are stored as C# files in your project, so they can be reviewed, edited, and tracked in source control.

blocks.title: How migrations work
blocks.text: EF Core compares your entity classes (the model) to a __EFMigrationsHistory table in the database. If the model has changed, EF Core generates a migration file containing the Up() and Down() methods to apply or reverse the schema changes.

The migration workflow has two steps: first, you generate a migration file by comparing the current model to the last migration; second, you apply the migration to the database by running the SQL it contains.

blocks.title: Migration workflow
items: Run 'dotnet ef migrations add <Name>' to generate a new migration file
Review the generated C# file to ensure it contains the expected schema changes
Run 'dotnet ef database update' to apply pending migrations to the database
To undo the last migration, run 'dotnet ef migrations remove' before applying it

blocks.title: Generating and applying migrations
blocks.content: CLI commands for managing the migration lifecycle.
blocks.code:
# Step 1: Add a new migration after changing the model
dotnet ef migrations add AddProductCategory

# Step 2: Review the generated migration file in Migrations/

# Step 3: Apply the migration to the database
dotnet ef database update

# If something went wrong, remove the last migration
dotnet ef migrations remove

blocks.text: When you run 'dotnet ef migrations add AddProductCategory', EF Core compares your entity classes to the last migration and generates a file with two methods: Up() adds the new column, and Down() removes it. This allows you to roll back the migration if needed.

blocks.title: Generated migration file example
blocks.content: What a typical migration file looks like after adding a Category column to the Product table.

blocks.text: Migrations support data seeding, which lets you insert initial data as part of a migration. This is useful for reference data like countries, product categories, or default user roles that your application needs to function.

blocks.title: Seeding product categories in a migration
blocks.content: Inserting initial category data as part of a migration using HasData.

blocks.title: Tip: Use explicit Id values for seeded data
blocks.text: When seeding data with HasData, always provide explicit primary key values. EF Core needs these keys to track whether the data already exists and whether to update or insert during migration.

terms.definition: The EF Core class that manages database connections, tracks entity changes, and coordinates queries and saves.
The service lifetime of DbContext. In ASP.NET Core, it is scoped (one instance per request).
A versioned schema change generated by EF Core to evolve the database model over time.
Methods in a migration file: Up() applies the change, Down() reverses it for rollbacks.
Inserting initial reference data as part of a migration so it is present on fresh databases.

blocks.title: Create and Apply Your First Migration
blocks.description: Add a new entity to an existing EF Core model, generate a migration, and apply it to the database.
steps: Create a new console project with EF Core and SQLite: 'dotnet new console -n MigrationDemo' and install the required packages
Define a Product entity with Id, Name, Price, and CreatedAt properties
Create a LibraryDbContext with DbSet<Product> and configure it to use SQLite with 'shop.db'
In Program.cs, create the database with context.Database.EnsureCreated() and add two sample products
Add a new Category entity with Id and Name properties, and add a DbSet<Category> to the context
Add a one-to-many relationship: a Category has many Products, and a Product belongs to one Category
Run 'dotnet ef migrations add AddCategories' and review the generated migration file
Run 'dotnet ef database update' to apply the migration, then query categories to verify the new table exists
blocks.expectedOutcome: The database now has a Categories table with a foreign key relationship to Products. The migration file correctly defines the Up() and Down() methods for creating and dropping the table and its foreign key.

blocks.title: DbContext and Migrations Summary
points: DbContext should be registered as scoped in ASP.NET Core for proper change tracking
AddDbContext<T> in Program.cs is the preferred way to configure DbContext for web apps
Migrations track schema changes over time as versioned C# files with Up() and Down() methods
Use 'dotnet ef migrations add' to generate migrations and 'dotnet ef database update' to apply them
Data seeding with HasData inserts initial reference data during migration
Never inject scoped DbContext into singleton services — it causes runtime errors
blocks.takeaway: Mastering DbContext configuration and the migration workflow is essential for maintaining database schemas alongside evolving application code. Migrations provide a reliable, version-controlled path from any schema state to the next.
